prompt: Each card is a statement a product team made after users with disabilities struggled with its service. Sort each statement by the model of disability it reflects.

cards.text: Customers who cannot hear the phone menu should get a better hearing aid before calling us.
cards.explanation: The problem is placed inside the person, as a deficit to be fixed.

cards.text: Our training videos exclude deaf staff because we never added captions, so we will add them to every video.
cards.explanation: The barrier is the design of the environment, and the fix is a design change.

cards.text: Applicants with a diagnosed condition can file a special request, and we will review it case by case.
cards.explanation: Access is granted as a specialized exception tied to a diagnosis rather than built into the design.

cards.text: The checkout fails for anyone who cannot use a mouse, so the checkout is what needs fixing.
cards.explanation: Disability is read as a mismatch between the person and an interface that could be designed otherwise.

cards.text: Our face-matching tool keeps rejecting users with facial palsy, so we will widen its evaluation set and change how it decides.
cards.explanation: The defect is located in the system's design and evaluation scope, not in the user.

cards.text: The voice assistant works fine. Some users simply have abnormal speech that it cannot be expected to handle.
cards.explanation: Users are framed as the anomaly, and the system's design is left unquestioned.

prompt: Each case describes an accessibility failure found in an audit. Identify which POUR principle it breaks.

cases.text: A pension website shows the projected balance only as a line chart, with no text description.
cases.explanation: Information carried only in a visual channel cannot be perceived by a screen-reader user.

cases.text: A bank's verification prompt locks the account if the code is not typed within 15 seconds, and the code field cannot be reached by keyboard.
cases.explanation: The control does not work by keyboard and imposes a punitive time limit.

cases.text: A loan chatbot explains a denial as 'adverse amortization covariance in your obligor profile' and offers no simpler wording.
cases.explanation: The explanation uses opaque jargon and cannot be adjusted in reading complexity.

cases.text: A store builds its buttons from unlabeled generic page elements, so braille displays announce them only as 'group'.
cases.explanation: Without standardized semantic markup, assistive technologies cannot parse the content reliably.

cases.text: A news app publishes AI-generated audio summaries with no transcript or captions.
cases.explanation: Generated audio needs captions or text so it can be perceived through another sensory channel.

cases.text: Each time a user scrolls, the insurance form reorders its fields and moves the submit button to a new place.
cases.explanation: Disorienting layout shifts make navigation unpredictable.

prompt: Each case describes an assistive AI tool going wrong. Identify the risk it shows.

cases.text: A shopper turns on large text and simplified layouts. Weeks later, an insurer that buys data from the retailer raises the shopper's quote.
cases.explanation: Use of accessibility features was logged as an inferred disability attribute and leaked into insurance scoring.

cases.text: A call centre gives an employee with dyslexia an eye-tracking reading aid, then uses its gaze logs to rank every agent's focus in performance reviews.
cases.explanation: Telemetry collected for support is repurposed for productivity surveillance.

cases.text: A banking assistant detects that a user relies on a screen reader and hides investment products from that user because they are 'too complex'.
cases.explanation: The system restricts options on assumptions about what the user can decide.

cases.text: A vision-to-speech app reads a pill bottle aloud and confidently states a dosage that is not printed on the label.
cases.explanation: A blind user cannot cross-check the fabricated detail visually.

cases.text: A university installs a typing-support tool for students with motor impairments, and the registrar starts using its keystroke records to flag 'disengaged' students.
cases.explanation: Assistive keystroke telemetry is turned to monitoring.

prompt: Each card describes a gap between two households using AI. Sort each card by the level of the digital divide it shows.

cards.text: One family shares a single phone with a capped data plan, while another has home fibre and a paid frontier-model subscription.
cards.explanation: The gap is in connectivity, hardware and the ability to pay for a frontier model.

cards.text: A student can afford only the ad-funded free tier of a chatbot, which runs a smaller model.
cards.explanation: Paying for frontier models versus relying on lower-capability free tiers is the access divide.

cards.text: Both neighbours use the same assistant, but only one knows to ask for sources and notices when an answer is invented.
cards.explanation: Recognizing hallucinations and verifying outputs is epistemic literacy.

cards.text: Two coworkers have the same tool, but only one knows how to raise its reasoning effort for hard questions.
cards.explanation: Configuring reasoning effort is a capability gap, not an access gap.

cards.text: Everyone in a town has access to AI, yet residents with configured shopping agents consistently pay lower all-in prices than residents who shop alone.
cards.explanation: Even with widespread access, those with advanced agents capture more market surplus.

cards.text: A firm with an AI agent settles billing disputes in a day, while individual customers of the same supplier wait weeks.
cards.explanation: Faster dispute resolution for the better equipped side is an outcome divide.

prompt: Each case describes a problem in a team that works with automation. Identify the concept it shows.

cases.text: A content filter flags 600 posts a night, nearly all harmless. Moderators begin clearing the queue with one click each without opening the posts.
cases.explanation: A high volume of false alarms conditions operators to dismiss without inspecting the evidence.

cases.text: After three years of reading scans with an AI assistant, a radiologist performs noticeably worse when the assistant is offline for a week.
cases.explanation: Relying on recommendations for routine cases let independent judgment atrophy.

cases.text: An autopilot handles almost every flight, then hands control to a rarely practiced pilot in a sudden storm with conflicting sensor readings.
cases.explanation: The more reliable the automation, the less practiced the human, yet the handed-back cases are the hardest.

cases.text: A loan clerk is disciplined for approving a loan the model scored as safe, though the clerk could never see the model's inputs or error range.
cases.explanation: The frontline employee absorbs liability for an opaque model they could not inspect.

cases.text: Delivery drivers who have used turn-by-turn routing for years can no longer plan a route across their own city from memory.
cases.explanation: Long reliance on automated guidance erodes the underlying skill.

prompt: Match each cognitive forcing function to the interface feature that applies it in an insurance claims review tool.

pairs.match: The adjuster must enter a payout decision from the claim file before the fraud score appears.
pairs.explanation: The reviewer records a provisional assessment before the model's score is revealed.

pairs.match: Claims on which the model's estimates are widely spread are outlined and marked for closer review.
pairs.explanation: Predictive dispersion is shown with the score, flagging low-consensus cases.

pairs.match: A button shows the two strongest signs the claim is genuine next to the two strongest signs it is not.
pairs.explanation: Evidence for both outcomes is presented instead of a one-sided summary.

prompt: Each card describes how a company involved users when building an AI hearing-test app. Sort each card by its rung group on the ladder of participation.

cards.text: The team scrapes posts from an online forum for deaf people to train the app, without asking the forum's members.
cards.explanation: Community data is taken with no participation at all.

cards.text: Instead of recruiting hard-of-hearing users, the team asks a language model to role-play twenty of them and reads the replies.
One week before launch, with the model frozen, the company invites deaf users to a single feedback session.
cards.explanation: Consultation comes after the design is locked, so participants cannot alter the system.

cards.text: The company posts a satisfaction survey for users with hearing loss but states that the results will not change the roadmap.
cards.explanation: Input is gathered with no authority attached to it.

cards.text: A paid advisory board of deaf users helps choose the training data and test prototypes, and it can block the launch.
cards.explanation: Compensated roles from scoping through testing, with veto authority.

cards.text: Audiologists and hard-of-hearing users co-write the app's success criteria and run its pre-launch red-team sessions.
cards.explanation: Affected users share power across the lifecycle, including pre-launch red-teaming.
